name: Emeka Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I repair power lines for an electricity company, usually in a bucket truck with a younger colleague. I have a vocational certificate and served an apprenticeship; after all these years I still put the tester on the line before believing a work order. I like leaving a house lit again and I dislike paperwork that eats the last hour of a shift. My partner Tessa and I have grown children, more than six months of expenses saved, and I have been thinking about retirement, although we have set no date. I use AI occasionally to tidy a report once the field readings are in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that a quicker report is fine if the isolation reading stays where a tired crew can see it. The pole still needs a person with a tester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My higher lineworker pay and the money we have saved mean this does not threaten our living. I would rather finish my remaining working years with a clear handover than argue with a new form every evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the repair rota and check any AI-written report against my pocket notebook. In the first year I would show the supervisor one report where the switch number or meter reading has been put in the wrong box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The work itself would barely move, and Tessa and I have room in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistake would be worth taking upstairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A switched pair of isolation numbers would be enough. A repair report should tell the next crew exactly which point was opened and tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tool more often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it saves the evening paperwork without hiding a reading. I am willing to use something that has proved itself on my own reports.

say: **Quicker reports** are fine when isolation readings remain easy to find.
**Physical testing** still decides whether a power line is safe.
think: Our **higher pay and savings** keep household income secure here.
Clear **handover records** matter more to me than a clever new form.
do: **Keep** line repair shifts and compare AI reports with pocket notes.
**Show** the supervisor a misplaced switch number or meter reading.
S0.quote: A repair report should tell the next crew exactly which point was opened and tested.
fieldNote: He is an **experienced mid-level** lineworker who repairs power lines, not a crew lead.
His **occasional AI use** remains tied to clearer reports after physical readings are taken.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and compare AI reports with pocket notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that dispatch and ordering will move before line repairs do. A faster route is useful only if it fits a bucket truck and leaves time to isolate the cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may ask fewer dispatchers to do more, and poor information could make our shifts longer. I do not expect my pay to vanish soon, with several utilities hiring nearby, but I would watch whether callout hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare six new route sheets with the drives we actually make. During the first year I would take any repeated mistake to the depot supervisor, then use the new route only if the field times stand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about extra pressure, not afraid of losing the house. The distinction matters when people start guessing at my retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What route error would matter most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lane to the old substation has a bridge too narrow for our truck. I would mark the detour and the time it takes to reach the fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your callout hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tessa and I would check our monthly bills before deciding to cut anything. With savings behind us, a short dip would not force a rushed retirement decision.

say: **Dispatch and ordering** change before hands-on line repair, which still needs bucket trucks and qualified workers.
**Bucket-truck access** must be included in route estimates.
think: Bad **office information** may lengthen shifts more than end my job.
Nearby **utilities** and savings reduce my immediate income risk.
do: **Compare** six route sheets with actual truck drives.
**Raise** repeated access errors with the depot supervisor before using new routes.
feel: **Uneasy** about time pressure, not expecting an immediate pay crisis.
S1.quote: A faster route is useful only if it fits a bucket truck and leaves time to isolate the cable.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **longer shifts** from immediate job loss.
His **savings** buy time to check bills, so no spending cut or early retirement is yet planned.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts while checking six new route sheets
Try new dispatch routes only after field times stand up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2028 could take the planning desk quickly, while robots able to do line repairs arrive about 2031. Our physical repairs would still need people in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be in my early sixties when the field robots arrive, and I had hoped to work a few more years if my health held. If the company cuts my repair shifts around 2031, the lost higher pay could change when Tessa and I can stop working, even with more than six months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a written account of our savings, bills and expected retirement income with Tessa this winter. If field shifts are cut after 2031 and the numbers show we can cover living costs, I would bring retirement forward; if they do not, I would apply to one of the nearby utilities for line repair work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the date. A forced end to good lineworker pay is different from choosing a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before retiring sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our regular bills, likely income and a margin for repairs at home would all have to fit. I would not use a good month of callouts as the number to build a retirement plan on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a nearby utility offers work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its wage and travel time with our monthly costs. I would take a suitable repair opening if retiring sooner did not add up.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches planning before capable repair robots around 2031.
**Physical crews** still work during that gap.
think: Reduced **repair shifts** around 2031 could end higher pay earlier than I planned.
More than **six months saved** gives choices but cannot settle a lifetime budget.
do: **Review** savings, regular bills and retirement income with Tessa.
**Retire** earlier if shifts fall after 2031 and full costs are covered.
**Apply** for nearby line repair work if earlier retirement does not add up.
feel: **Anxious** about a forced loss of good pay near retirement.
S2.quote: A forced end to good lineworker pay is different from choosing a retirement date.
fieldNote: He would **retire earlier** only after both a shift cut and an affordable lifetime budget.
His fallback is a **nearby line job**, conditional on the retirement numbers failing.

steps.text: Bring retirement forward if shifts fall after 2031 and living costs remain covered
Apply for nearby line repair if earlier retirement does not cover costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives the utility time to tell crews what line work will still be done by people. Thinking AI comes by 2031, with capable field robots around 2034, so the dates should not be blurred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be around sixty-three when the office changes and around sixty-six when robots reach physical repairs. We might have reached a comfortable retirement by then, but I cannot promise that until Tessa and I check our actual finances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the line repair job and review retirement costs with Tessa each year. If we can afford the date we choose, I would leave work before field robots arrive around 2034; if not, I would keep repairing lines and check nearby utility openings if hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Careful, with less urgency than the 2028 picture. A robot launch is no pension plan for a lineworker with bills to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the chosen date affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would need ordinary bills covered without assuming every year brings callout pay. I would leave extra room for home maintenance before writing a date on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take robot training to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try a short paid course if my employer offered it and I needed the skill for continued line work. I would not pay for a long new qualification this close to a possible retirement.

say: **2031 office AI** and field robots around 2034 leave different time for crews.
**Retirement dates** should follow household numbers, not a launch schedule.
think: A **comfortable retirement** by 2034 is possible but not certain.
I may still need **repair wages** if normal bills exceed the plan.
do: **Review** retirement costs with Tessa each year while repairing lines.
**Try** employer-paid robot controls course if needed for continuing work.
**Leave** before 2034 if finances allow; otherwise keep repairs and check utility openings if hours fall.
feel: **Careful**, with time to choose a date from real finances.
S3.quote: A robot launch is no pension plan for a lineworker with bills to pay.
fieldNote: He links **retirement timing** to audited household costs, without assuming a guaranteed pension.
He would take **paid controls training** only if he remains in line repair and the employer offers it.

steps.text: Keep repairing lines and review retirement costs with Tessa annually
Take paid robot controls course if needed for continuing line work
Leave line work before 2034 if retirement income covers household costs
Check nearby utility openings if retirement unaffordable and hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade takes the field robots to around 2039, when I would be in my seventies. Thinking AI in 2036 may tidy the office first, but I do not need to plan a second trade to get through another ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to retire before the robots reach the poles if our finances keep to plan. Even so, I would not tell a younger crew that a machine safety rule is someone else’s problem; they will live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current repair shifts for now and revisit the retirement plan with Tessa each year. In the first year after 2036, if I am still working, I would join the company crew meeting on robot stop rules; if retired, I would leave the rulemaking to the people doing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about my own income and schedule. I feel responsible for handing on useful habits before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which habit would you pass on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach the newest worker to check the isolation point against the actual label, even when a machine printed the work order. A wrong isolation label can turn a quick power-line repair into a dangerous one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move retirement earlier because of the 2039 robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would follow the date our bills support, and the robot date alone would not make me leave before that.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes office work before field robots around 2039.
**Junior crews** will need clear stop and isolation rules.
think: I expect **retirement** before field robots reach poles if finances hold.
The **robot date** alone would not bring retirement forward.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and review retirement finances with Tessa annually.
**Join** the crew robot stop-rule meeting after 2036 only if still working.
feel: **Calm** about personal income, mindful of younger workers.
S4.quote: A wrong isolation label can turn a quick power-line repair into a dangerous one.
fieldNote: He expects a **long runway** to pass his intended retirement window, subject to finances.
He keeps **stop-rule participation** conditional on actually working with a line crew after 2036.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and review retirement finances annually
Join crew stop-rule meeting after 2036 if still working

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because field robots around 2031 could cut my good repair hours before Tessa and I have decided whether retirement is affordable. A clear account of the household bills and access to nearby utility openings would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether older workers get a choice when shifts are reduced. I would want a discussion about reduced line repair shifts before a rota arrives with my name missing.

portrait: **Emeka Jensen**, 58, is an experienced mid-level lineworker with a vocational certificate and apprenticeship.
He has **higher pay**, more than six months saved, a partner and grown children, with retirement coming into view.
He uses **AI occasionally** for reports, but checks the switching and meter details against his pocket notebook.
In **Steady Disruption**, he expects time pressure rather than immediate income loss and checks truck routes against reality.
The **2028 picture** worries him because field robots could shorten his high-pay years before a retirement plan is affordable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his repair hours around 2031 before a financially sound retirement date is chosen.
whatWouldHelp: A detailed **household budget** would show whether stopping earlier is affordable.
Access to **nearby repair openings** could protect income if early retirement does not add up.
headlineQuote: I would want a discussion about reduced line repair shifts before a rota arrives with my name missing.
